opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what long context is actually for. When people first talked about long context, it was almost a benchmark game: can you fit a whole book, can you find the needle in the haystack. But the real use case now is agents. An agent working on a real task, writing code across a repository, browsing, calling tools, reflecting on its own mistakes, accumulates context continuously. The trajectory just keeps growing. So long context is no longer an occasional feature. It's the default working state of the model.

Once you see it that way, cost and speed stop being nice-to-haves. With standard attention, every additional token you generate has to look back at everything before it, and the KV cache grows linearly with length. At a few thousand tokens nobody cares. At hundreds of thousands of tokens, across many steps of an agent loop, and across many users at the same time, that cost dominates everything. If each step is slow and expensive, the agent can't afford to think long, explore, or retry, and those are exactly the things that make it capable.

There's also a feedback loop with training. Reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks means you're doing huge amounts of rollout, which is basically inference. If inference is cheap and fast, you can run more rollouts, longer ones, and the model learns more from the same compute budget. So efficient inference isn't only a serving concern. It directly shapes how good the model can become.

That's why I see it as enduring rather than a temporary engineering problem. Hardware will get better, but our ambitions for context length and task length grow faster than hardware does. Whenever things get cheaper, people immediately use the slack to do longer, more complex tasks. So the architecture has to be designed from the start with efficiency in mind: things like compressing the KV cache, sparse or selective attention, and hybrid designs where not every layer pays the full quadratic cost. The goal is that the model only spends compute on the parts of the context that actually matter.

In a way, I think the competition in long-context architecture isn't really about who supports the longest window on paper. It's about who can make long context cheap enough that people actually use it all the time. That's what turns a capability into something useful in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response explains that cheaper, faster inference lets people use longer and more complex tasks, and says architecture must make long context cheap enough for routine use.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that all current model architectures can be trained to support a context length of 100 million tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that cost and speed are the things that determine whether long context is actually used, not whether it exists on a slide.

When we started looking seriously at long-context architecture, the question everyone asked was "can the model handle a million tokens?" And technically, you can push context length up with enough compute. But the real question is what it costs to serve that, every single request, in production. Attention is quadratic, the KV cache grows linearly with length, and both of those hit you at inference time, not just training. If a user puts in a long document or a long codebase and the response takes twenty seconds and costs ten times a normal request, that feature is dead on arrival. People will chunk it, summarize it, do retrieval instead. So the capability gets designed around rather than used.

That's why I say these are enduring priorities, not a temporary engineering concern. The length people want keeps growing. Agents accumulate history over many turns. Code repositories are huge. Multi-document reasoning is the natural use case. Every one of those pushes toward longer context, and every one of those makes the cost problem worse, not better. Hardware improvements help, but demand grows faster than hardware does. So if you don't bake efficiency into the architecture itself, you end up paying for it forever at the serving layer.

The other thing I'd say is that cheap and fast inference changes how you train, too. If inference is expensive, you can't afford to generate lots of long-context data, run long rollouts for reinforcement learning, or let the model think for many steps. Efficient inference unlocks the training loop. So in our thinking it was never "make it good first, then make it cheap later." The two have to be designed together, because the architecture decisions you make about attention, about how you compress or share the KV cache, about sparsity, those are very hard to retrofit once the model is trained.

So for me, low cost and fast inference aren't a constraint on long context. They're the condition for it to matter at all.

r001.rationale: The response explains that rising context lengths make inference costs worse and says efficiency must be built into the architecture for long context to be practical, conveying that low cost and fast inference enable much longer contexts.

r002.rationale: The response mentions that context can be pushed to a million tokens with enough compute, but it does not claim that all current architectures can be trained to support 100 million tokens.

astra-6.text:
Because as models become more capable, we keep asking them to process more information. Any efficiency gain gets used to support longer context, more users, or more complex tasks. So cost and latency don’t disappear as concerns when hardware improves.

Long context makes this particularly important. Being able to accept a very long input is only part of the problem. You also have to process it efficiently, keep the necessary state in memory, and generate an answer quickly enough to be useful. An architecture can perform well on a benchmark but still be too expensive to deploy at that context length.

That’s why I see efficiency as a fundamental architectural goal. We want models that can use more context effectively while keeping the cost of serving them manageable. That determines how broadly people can actually use the capability.

r001.rationale: It says efficiency gains support longer context and that models can use more context effectively while keeping serving costs manageable.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim that all current architectures can be trained for a 100-million-token context.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a longer context is only useful if people can afford to use it and the model responds quickly enough. As the context grows, the model has more information to process and retain, so both computation and memory become constraints. Supporting a very long sequence is one thing; making it practical for everyday use is another.

That’s why I see cost and inference speed as lasting architectural priorities. Even as hardware improves, we’ll ask models to handle longer documents, more conversation history, and more complex tasks. The demand grows too. We need architectures that use those resources efficiently while preserving the model’s ability to find and reason over relevant information. The goal is useful long-context capability at a cost and latency people can actually work with.

r001.rationale: The response says efficient cost and inference speed make long-context capability practical as context lengths grow.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that all current model architectures can be trained to support 100 million tokens.
